title: Enforcing democratic norms through reciprocal transgressions
why: Argues that answering a breach of democratic rules with a matching breach can help keep the norms in force, under constraints. Reciprocity as enforcement, next to Rawls's reciprocity as justification.
summary: Lepoutre asks when citizens or officials may answer a rival's breach of democratic rules with a breach of their own. He argues that tit-for-tat responses can help keep fair democratic standards in force and need not start a spiral of retaliation. Such responses face their own limits on timing, method and who may act.

title: Just Savings, Compensation, and the First Generation
venue: Journal of Ethics and Social Philosophy
why: Proposes compensating the first generation through the younger generations it overlaps with, as an alternative to Rawls's just savings principle.
summary: Rawls needs to explain why rational contractors would adopt a saving rule that burdens the first and poorest generation. Wiseman argues that the existing rationales miss a better one: later generations repay the early savers. He defends a saving rule with repayment as the one the original position would favour.

title: What Do Mini-Publics Prove?
why: Asks whether successful mini-publics show that lottocracy would work, and what they show about citizens' political competence.
summary: Kogelmann asks whether the success of mini-publics shows that lottocracy, rule by citizens chosen by lot, would work. He treats the step as an inference about external validity and tests it against social science and philosophy of science. Mini-publics say little about how lottocracy would operate, though they do show what ordinary people can do.

title: Between corporate values and grandstanding: The compatibility of corporate activism with democracy
why: Holds that worries about corporate activism are overstated when the activism is integral to the business, and that the incidental kind is often grandstanding.
summary: Frye asks whether businesses that take public stands on social and political issues undermine democracy. He argues the worry is overstated once activism that comes from a firm's identity is separated from opportunistic posturing. The real democratic problem lies in the pressures that make corporate views uniform and feed polarization.

title: Scaling Laws and the Fair-Use Proviso on Urban Territory
why: Uses urban scaling laws to argue that local control of land use is likely to violate fair-use provisos, which puts it at odds with egalitarianism.
summary: Monaghan asks whether territorial rights can justify local control of urban land use, given a fairness condition on claiming space. He argues that the scaling laws that govern cities make local control likely to violate that condition, which puts it at odds with egalitarian commitments.

title: Standing duties over time: Operation-bounded responsibility and historical injustice
authors: Wenxuan Hou [University of Edinburgh; Brown University]
why: Duties to repair historical injustice persist and vary with the wrong's continuing effects, and can be completed without the wrong being erased.
summary: Hou asks whether duties to repair a past wrong end with the wrong or continue. Hou argues that standing reparative duties last until the harm they target is undone, growing and shrinking with it. This operation-bounded responsibility explains the obligations of historical injustice without treating the wrong as erased.

title: Escaping the understanding-assent links impasse
why: Offers an account of radical deviance, on which a speaker refuses the dialectic that gives a word its meaning. The understanding-assent debate is the current form of the dispute over analyticity, which connects it to the Carnap thread.
summary: Walerius asks whether a speaker who rejects the practice that fixes a word's content counts as radically deviant, and argues that such a speaker does. The answer shows how externalists can exclude some speakers from a practice, and it offers a way around the standoff over links between understanding and assent.

title: Two Ways to Think About (Implicit) Structure
why: Compares invariance-based and definability-based accounts of implicit structure and links them formally. Relevant to what a structural reconstruction commits you to.
summary: Schiemer asks how best to capture the implicit structure of mathematical systems. He contrasts an approach through definability, set in formal languages and model theory, with an approach through invariance. Using finite geometry and relational algebra, he examines how the two are connected and considers equivalence by bi-interpretability.

title: Substitutional Quantification and Arithmetical Truth
why: Defends substitutional quantification against Kripke's equivalence claim and uses it to explain a determinate notion of arithmetical truth.
summary: Warren asks whether substitutional quantification is a viable option and argues against the widely accepted claim that it collapses into objectual quantification. He then uses substitutional quantifiers, together with one further principle, to explain how speakers come to grasp a determinate notion of arithmetical truth.

title: Reference, conflicting intentions, and the Madagascar problem
why: Explains the Madagascar reference shift through conflicting name-using intentions whose relative strengths change over time.
summary: Koch and Raimondi take up the Madagascar problem: how a name can change its referent. A speaker can use a name with conflicting intentions, and when the weaker intention becomes dominant the name's reference shifts in that speaker's idiolect. Deference spreads the shift through the community. The account stays within the causal-historical framework.

title: Referring without a single target: Demonstratives, intentionalism, and partial intentions
authors: Seungtaek Lee [University of California, Los Angeles]
why: A weaker intentionalism: a demonstrative can refer without a single target fixed in advance, by way of partial intentions.
summary: Lee asks whether a speaker can refer with a demonstrative while undecided among several objects. Lee argues that a weaker intentionalism allows it, with reference grounded in partial intentions and no single fixed target. The argument draws on action theory and an existing account of felicitous underspecification.

title: The semantics-pragmatics divide in cartographic representation
authors: Francesco Pierini [Università degli Studi di Genova]
why: Argues against literalism about maps: pragmatics shapes their truth conditions throughout. Also bears on depiction.
summary: Pierini asks whether the rules that assign content to a map's marks settle its truth conditions alone, or whether context also plays a part. He rejects the literalist view, using Google Maps examples to argue that pragmatics changes a map's semantic components. The result supports contextualism about maps.

title: Context shift and viewpoint shift: Super Monsters revisited
authors: Philippe Schlenker, Jason Lamberton, Jonathan Lamberton
why: Formal semantics of context shift, returning to the super-monster cases.

title: Pluralism, parity, and justification intransitivity
why: Parity and intransitivity together in the title: the closest match this month to the Muñoz and Chang pairing in your October issue.

title: Requiring vs. justifying: derived, not basic
why: Defends the dual-ranking model of reasons but derives the requiring and justifying roles from a single dimension of weight.
summary: Schroeder defends the dual ranking model of reasons, on which requiring and justifying come apart, but denies that the distinction is basic. He argues that both roles can be explained through a single dimension of weight, so the difference between requiring and justifying is derived.

title: A Reason Itself Neither Requires nor Permits: On an Alleged Distinction between Two Roles for Reasons
why: The case against the two-roles distinction. Gert's reply to Berker is listed next.

title: On some alleged problems for the distinction between two roles for reasons
why: Replies to Berker: the objections come from interpretive moves that are mistaken or optional, not from flaws in the distinction.
summary: Gert replies to Berker's objections to the distinction between two roles for reasons, requiring and justifying. He argues that the worries dissolve once counterfactual, motivational and monistic misreadings of the distinction are set aside. Moral, legal and practical reasons are then distinguished by the normative statuses they affect.

title: Quo vadis, reasons first? From weight monism to weight pluralism to thresholds
why: Finds problems for weight pluralism and explores a threshold version of reasons-first monism as the alternative.
summary: Schmidt tests a reasons-first view with a single kind of weight against supererogation, latitude, dilemmas, and the difference between requirement and ought. Weight monism struggles with these, but weight pluralism has troubles of its own. She then explores a version of the view built on thresholds.

title: On the Match by Closeness Approach to Limited Aggregation
why: Limited aggregation is a neighbouring problem to value comparison.

title: Improving Lives and Avoiding Harm
authors: Tim Campbell [Institute for Futures Studies], Patrick Kaczmarek [University of St Andrews]
why: Argues that every harm-avoidance account of the Asymmetry in population ethics runs into serious problems.
summary: Campbell and Kaczmarek examine theories that explain the asymmetry in population ethics by appeal to harm avoidance alone. They argue that every such theory, however refined, must accept one of four unattractive consequences, and that any reasonable account of the asymmetry faces the same choice.

title: Expressivism and Evidence for Moral Judgments
why: Expressivists can make sense of evidence for moral judgements by reading evidence claims as first-order questions about permissible standards.
summary: Valencia Pacheco asks whether expressivism, which treats moral judgments as expressions of attitude, can make room for evidence that supports them. He argues that it can if expressivists begin with talk of evidence: saying that one thing is evidence for another expresses a normative standard. Questions about moral evidence become first-order normative questions.

title: Metaethics and practical reason, as usual
why: Published alongside Williamson's synopsis of Good as Usual, which is listed next.

title: Synopsis of Good as Usual: Anti-Exceptionalist Essays on Values, Norms, and Action
why: Williamson's own summary of his essays on values, norms and action.

title: On Permissive Consent
why: Treats consenting as asserting that the act is permissible, which puts it between ethics and speech-act theory.
summary: Dinges asks what it is to give consent, the act that can make an otherwise wrongful act permissible. He proposes that to consent is to assert a normative claim: that the act is permissible. The view is set against accounts that require communicating an intention and accounts that require no communication at all.

title: Epistemic supererogation and the right to believe
why: By the author of On the logic of what matters, from your October issue.

title: Defending ontic structural realism in quantum field theory
why: Structural realism, at the edge of the theoretical-terms thread. Philosophy of physics more than language.
summary: Meyer asks whether intrinsic properties in quantum field theory refute ontic structural realism. Meyer argues that they do not: the properties in question may not be intrinsic after all, and if they are, the structural realist can accommodate them.

title: Metasemantics and the Continuum Hypothesis
authors: Neil Alexander Barton [National University of Singapore]
why: Metasemantics applied to set theory: how thought about the Continuum Hypothesis can vary across agents and stay determinate.
summary: Barton asks how disagreement about the Continuum Hypothesis is possible when thinkers conceive of it differently. He argues that moderate theories of content reject the assumption that thought about the hypothesis is uniform across agents, and that the hypothesis can still be determinate for each thinker.

title: Conversing without asserting: chatbots as interlocutors
why: Speech-act theory applied to chatbots: conversation through acts that fall short of assertion.
summary: Michel and Green ask what chatbots do when they converse. They argue that chatbots perform proto-assertoric acts, which they call ursertions and semisertions. These acts can be assessed for correctness and advance a shared conversational goal, but they carry no assertoric commitment.

title: Reasoning about risk and the Sure-thing Postulate
why: Decision theory: argues against Savage's Sure-thing Postulate. Adjacent to the value-comparison thread.
summary: Kernohan asks whether Savage's model of rational choice survives its treatment of information about lotteries. He argues that summary features such as modes and medians can properly guide choice and sometimes conflict with the Sure-thing Postulate. The conflicts undermine the postulate and with it Savage's case for subjective expected utility and Bayesian probabilism.

title: Periodic Equity Prioritarianism
authors: Susumu Cato [The University of Tokyo], Anders Herlitz [Lund University; Institute for Futures Studies]
why: A prioritarian view for people who are differently well off at different times.
summary: Cato and Herlitz ask how prioritarianism should treat people who fare unevenly across the stages of their lives. They propose periodic equity prioritarianism, which adapts a technique from decision under uncertainty. They argue that it avoids the problems facing both timeslice and whole-life versions of the view.

title: No determinate facts, no objective oughts?
why: Tests two objectivist accounts of what we ought to do under metaphysical indeterminacy and finds that both fail.
summary: Marra and Tiefensee ask whether there can be objective oughts where the relevant facts are not determinate. They examine two proposals an objectivist might make to secure such oughts and argue that neither works.

title: Autonomy: how lesser goods can be justifying reasons
why: From the same exchange on requiring and justifying reasons: how autonomy grounds permissible partiality.
summary: Tucker argues that autonomy can justify choosing a lesser good, for instance dining out over giving to an effective charity. The justification does not reduce autonomy to wellbeing or to attitudes open to assessment. Lesser goods can therefore serve as justifying reasons.

title: Duty and permission for utilitarians
why: A rule-utilitarian account of the difference between justifying and requiring reasons.
summary: Huemer gives a rule-utilitarian account of duty and permission. The best social rules must make room for partiality, so they supply justifications for declining to sacrifice oneself and set limits on how demanding morality can be.

title: A Defense of Affirmative Action for Conservatives
why: Argues that academic affirmative action for conservatives is defensible. In your area, away from your threads.
summary: Jacobson asks whether preferring conservatives in academic admissions and hiring would be unjust. He argues that it would not, since conservatives already face discrimination there. He adds that a wider range of viewpoints would improve academic life as a whole and not only benefit heterodox scholars.

title: Ignorance and Indifference of the Deaths of (Select) Others
why: Explains unequal concern for civilians killed in different wars, testing racism explanations against a Marxist account of imperialism.
summary: Dror asks why Westerners care more about civilian deaths in some foreign wars than in others. Dror finds explanations from racism insufficient, whether as individual hostility or as structural white ignorance, and argues that a Marxist account of imperialism explains the pattern better. Race and imperialism are treated as intertwined.

title: Toward an Ontology of Nations
why: Social ontology that political philosophy may draw on.

title: Coordinating Mental Imagery
authors: Silvana Pani [University of Milan; University of Bergamo]
why: Imagination more than aesthetics, but the nearest item to that area in this window.
summary: Pani asks whether mental imagery, which seems private to each person, can support coordination between people. She argues that agents can align their imagining without having identical episodes or matching contents, by relying on mutual constraints and joint aims. Work on shared perception and joint action supports the view.

title: The roles of religious conviction in a publicly justified polity
why: The convergence view of public justification. The October review of Rawls left one concern standing: why shared reasons and not convergence.
summary: They defend a convergence view of public justification: a coercive law is justified only if each citizen has sufficient reason of their own to accept it. Religious reasons can therefore defeat a law for those who hold them, though they cannot justify imposing one on others, and duties of restraint fall differently on citizens and officials.

title: How to Define Theoretical Terms
why: The Ramsey and Carnap method in its standard later form. Background to both Psillos and De Benedetto and La Rosa.
summary: Lewis shows how to define a theory's new terms from its old vocabulary. Replace the theoretical terms with variables to form the Ramsey sentence, then define each term as naming the corresponding member of the theory's unique realization, if there is one. Theoretical terms become definable and eliminable without loss.

title: Counterexamples to the transitivity of better than
why: Argues from spectrum cases that better than is not transitive, the kind of intuition Muñoz reassigns to defeat.
summary: Rachels argues that better than is not transitive. In a sequence of pains, each slightly milder but much longer than the last, every step seems worse than the one before, yet the final long discomfort seems better than the brief agony at the start. He defends these judgments against attempts to explain them away.

title: Aesthetic Concepts
why: The account of aesthetic concepts that Walton's Categories of Art responds to.
summary: Sibley argues that aesthetic terms such as graceful or garish are not governed by conditions: no list of non-aesthetic features is ever enough to guarantee that one applies. Applying them takes taste, and critics support their judgments by getting others to see the features, not by proof.

title: Critical Notice: Bertrand Russell's The Analysis of Matter: Its Historical Context and Contemporary Interest
why: Revives Newman's objection to structural content and links it to Ramsey sentences. Background to the Newman challenge in the Psillos review.
summary: Demopoulos and Friedman revive Newman's 1928 objection to Russell's structuralism: a theory that says only that relations of a given structure exist is true whenever the world has enough objects. They find the same difficulty in Ramsey-sentence accounts of theories and in Putnam's model-theoretic argument.

title: Value Incommensurability: Some Preliminaries
why: Gives an account of incommensurability and a test for it based on failures of transitivity in comparisons. Bears on incomparability and parity.
summary: Raz calls two options incommensurable when neither is better and they are not of equal value. The mark is a failure of transitivity: improving one option does not make it better than the other. He argues that such incommensurability is common and is no defect in the options or in what is known of them.
